Hyperbolic pair (B(e,f)=1)

Words: 51
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
Two vectors spanning a hyperbolic plane. For an alternating bilinear form, choose B(e,f)=1; then their span is nondegenerate. For a quadratic form with polar form B, require also Q(e)=Q(f)=0. The analogous definition for a Hermitian form uses two isotropic vectors of pairing one. Extending such pairs to adapted bases is useful for constructing form-preserving maps.

Cartesian basis

Words: 15
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A Cartesian basis is an orthonormal basis associated with the perpendicular axes of a Cartesian coordinate system.

Bilinear form

Words: 1k Articles: 31
Linear algebra OurBigBook.com
A bilinear form on a vector space V over a field F is a map B:V×V→F that is linear in each argument separately.

Orthogonal complement for a bilinear form (W⊥={v:B(w,v)=0 for all w∈W})

Words: 69
Bilinear form OurBigBook.com
For a bilinear form on a finite-dimensional vector space, the displayed right bilinear orthogonal complement is a subspace. Nondegeneracy identifies the ambient space with its dual and gives dimW⊥=dimV−dimW. If the form is symmetric or alternating, orthogonality is reciprocal and (W⊥)⊥=W. For a general nonsymmetric form, left and right complements must be distinguished. A restricted symmetric or alternating form has radical of a bilinear form W∩W⊥; quotienting by that radical of a bilinear form gives a nondegenerate induced form.

Isometry of a space with a form

Words: 150 Articles: 2
Bilinear form OurBigBook.com
A linear bijection between spaces carrying compatible bilinear forms, Hermitian forms or quadratic forms is an isometry of a space with a form when it preserves the specified form. Preserving the polar form alone need not preserve a quadratic form in characteristic two. Subspaces may have degenerate restricted forms even when the ambient form is nonsingular.

Anisotropic vector for a form

Words: 49
Isometry of a space with a form OurBigBook.com
A vector is anisotropic for a quadratic form if Q(v)=0, and for a Hermitian form if h(v,v)=0. The complementary zero-value condition is isotropy. For a symmetric bilinear form in odd characteristic of a field, this agrees with the associated quadratic form. A nondegenerate alternating bilinear form has all self-pairings zero, so nondegeneracy must not be confused with the existence of anisotropic vectors.

Witt's theorem

Words: 59
Isometry of a space with a form OurBigBook.com
An isometry of a space with a form between subspaces of a finite-dimensional nonsingular classical space extends to an ambient isometry. This includes alternating bilinear forms in all characteristics, symmetric bilinear forms in characteristic different from two, Hermitian forms with nontrivial involution, and quadratic forms with nonsingular polar form. No nonsingularity of the restricted subspace is required. Bare nonalternating symmetric bilinear forms in characteristic two require additional hypotheses and must not be confused with quadratic spaces.

Positive-definite bilinear form (B(v,v)>0(v=0))

Words: 80 Articles: 1
Bilinear form OurBigBook.com
A symmetric real bilinear form is positive-definite when B(v,v)>0 for every nonzero vector. It defines an inner product and the associated norm B(v,v)​. The complex Killing form is not positive-definite on the entire complex Cartan subalgebra; its restriction to the Euclidean subspace of a Cartan subalgebra is a real positive-definite form.

Positive definiteness (q(v)>0(v=0))

Words: 42
Positive-definite bilinear form OurBigBook.com
The strict positivity of a quadratic form on every nonzero vector. A real symmetric matrix has positive definiteness exactly when its associated quadratic form does, making it a positive-definite matrix. A Hermitian form is positive definite when its value on (v,v) is real and strictly positive for every nonzero vector.

Alternating bilinear form (B(v,v)=0)

Words: 51
Bilinear form OurBigBook.com
A bilinear form is alternating if B(v,v)=0 for every vector v. Expanding B(v+w,v+w) implies B(v,w)=−B(w,v). The converse requires characteristic different from two. In that characteristic a skew-symmetric matrix of odd integer size has zero determinant, since detA=det(−AT)=(−1)ndetA. Thus an alternating form on a finite odd-dimensional vector space is degenerate. A nondegenerate alternating form defines a symplectic vector space.

Symmetric bilinear form

Words: 128 Articles: 2
Bilinear form OurBigBook.com
A bilinear form B is symmetric when B(v,w)=B(w,v) for every pair of vectors v,w.

Modified trace form on real matrices (ϕ(A,B)=tr(AB)−tr(A)tr(B))

Words: 66
Symmetric bilinear form OurBigBook.com
On real n by n matrices with n≥2, split into traceless symmetric matrices, skew-symmetric matrices and scalar matrices. These summands are orthogonal for the displayed symmetric bilinear form. The form is positive on the first summand, negative on the second and negative on the scalar identity direction. Its inertia of a bilinear form is (n(n+1)/2−1,n(n−1)/2+1,0), its rank is n2 and its signature is n−2. Indeed tr(S2)=∥S∥F2​, tr(K2)=−∥K∥F2​ and ϕ(tI,tI)=−n(n−1)t2.

Witt group of a field (W(K))

Words: 49
Symmetric bilinear form OurBigBook.com
For a field K of characteristic different from two, W(K) is the group of nonsingular symmetric bilinear forms modulo metabolic forms, with orthogonal sum as addition. A metabolic form has a half-dimensional totally isotropic subspace. Such a form is equivalent to a sum of hyperbolic planes, hence represents zero.

Words: 242 Articles: 4
Bilinear form OurBigBook.com
A bilinear form B:X×X→R on a normed vector space is bounded when some C<∞ satisfies ∣B(u,v)∣≤C∥u∥∥v∥ for all u,v∈X.

Grothendieck inequality

Words: 180 Articles: 2
Bounded bilinear form OurBigBook.com
For a finite real scalar matrix (aij​) and unit vectors ui​,vj​ in a real Hilbert space, ∣∑aij​⟨ui​,vj​⟩∣≤KG​maxεi​,δj​∈{−1,1}​∣∑aij​εi​δj​∣, with a universal constant. One valid bound is KG​≤π/(2log(1+2​)). Expand sin(ct) using odd tensor powers with coefficient magnitudes summing to sinhc=1, then apply the Gaussian sign identity E[sgn⟨G,u⟩sgn⟨G,v⟩]=(2/π)arcsin⟨u,v⟩. Taking c=log(1+2​) converts the expectation back to the original inner product. Complex scalars admit a universal bound twice this real bound by separating real and imaginary parts.
Grothendieck theorem for L1 to Hilbert operators
Words: 98 Articles: 1
Grothendieck inequality OurBigBook.com
Every bounded linear operator T:L1(μ)→H into a Hilbert space is an absolutely summing operator, with π1​(T)≤KG​∥T∥. For simple functions on a common disjoint partition, apply the Grothendieck inequality to the vectors T(1A​/μ(A)) and norming vectors of the images. The scalar sign or phase supremum is the weak 1-norm of the family. Approximation by simple functions proves the general result.
Rademacher span is not complemented in L1
Words: 45
Grothendieck theorem for L1 to Hilbert operators OurBigBook.com
If the closed span of the Rademacher functions were a complemented subspace of L1(0,1), compose a projection with the inverse of its l2 sequence space parametrization. The Grothendieck theorem for L1 to Hilbert operators would make this map an absolutely summing operator. Its composition with the parametrization would make the identity on the infinite-dimensional l2 sequence space absolutely summing, contradicting its coordinate-vector test.

Bounded bilinear form OurBigBook.com
A bilinear form on a normed vector space is continuous exactly when it is bounded. For the nontrivial direction, continuity at (0,0) gives r,s>0 such that ∣B(x,y)∣≤1 whenever ∥x∥<r and ∥y∥<s; scaling nonzero u,v into these balls gives ∣B(u,v)∣≤4(rs)−1∥u∥∥v∥.

Dual isomorphisms induced by a nondegenerate pairing (U≅V∗,V≅U∗)

Words: 69
Nondegenerate bilinear form OurBigBook.com
A bilinear form b:U×V→K with zero left and right radicals induces injective linear maps U→V∗ and V→U∗. Finite dimensions force dimU=dimV, so both maps are isomorphisms. For any other bilinear form c, composing its maps to the dual spaces with these inverse isomorphisms gives unique endomorphisms S,T with c(x,y)=b(Sx,y)=b(x,Ty). In bases with invertible pairing matrix B and coefficient matrix C, S=B−TCT and T=B−1C.

Symplectic vector space

Words: 351 Articles: 7
Nondegenerate bilinear form OurBigBook.com
A symplectic vector space is a vector space equipped with a nondegenerate antisymmetric bilinear form. Every finite-dimensional symplectic vector space has even dimension: splitting off one symplectic two-plane leaves a smaller nondegenerate antisymmetric space, and induction completes the decomposition.
Symplectic linear map (A∗ωW​=ωV​)
Words: 42
Symplectic vector space OurBigBook.com
A linear map A:(V,ωV​)→(W,ωW​) is symplectic when it pulls back the target symplectic form to the source form. Nondegenerate bilinear form makes such a map injective. In equal finite dimensions it is an isomorphism. The automorphisms form the symplectic group and preserve the symplectic orientation on the ambient space and on every symplectic subspace.
Symplectic subspace
Words: 97 Articles: 1
Symplectic vector space OurBigBook.com
A subspace of a symplectic vector space is symplectic if the restricted symplectic form is nondegenerate. It has a symplectic orthogonal complement and the ambient space is the direct sum of those two subspaces.
Orientation criterion for a graph of symplectic planes (ω∣ΓA​​=(1+detA)ωD​)
Words: 71
Symplectic subspace OurBigBook.com
Let V=C⊕D be a symplectic orthogonal complement splitting into two symplectic subspaces of dimension two. In symplectic bases, the graph of a function A:D→C pulls back the symplectic form to ωD​+A∗ωC​=(1+detA)ωD​. It is a symplectic subspace exactly when detA=−1. Its symplectic orientation agrees with the orientation transported from D exactly when detA>−1. When detA<−1, the transverse oriented pair (C,ΓA​) has negative intersection sign, whereas two distinct complex lines in a compatible complex two-space have positive intersection sign.
Eigenspaces of a symplectic involution (V=V+​⊕V−​)

Symplectic vector space OurBigBook.com
If T preserves a nondegenerate bilinear form ω that is alternating and satisfies T2=I on a finite-dimensional vector space over a field of characteristic different from two, then
V=ker(T−I)⊕ker(T+I).
(3)
The two eigenspaces are orthogonal for ω, since ω(v+​,v−​)=ω(Tv+​,Tv−​)=−ω(v+​,v−​). Each restricted form is nondegenerate: a vector annihilating its own eigenspace also annihilates the other and hence all of V. Both dimensions are even, say 2a and 2b. Consequently trT=2a−2b=dimV−4b as an integer obtained from the eigenspace dimensions. Over the real numbers this gives the congruence trT≡dimV(mod4).

The symplectic orthogonal complement of a subspace W is Wω={v:ω(v,w)=0 for every w∈W}. The nondegenerate bilinear form gives dimWω=dimV−dimW. An isotropic subspace of a symplectic vector space satisfies W⊂Wω; a Lagrangian subspace satisfies equality.

Symplectic vector space OurBigBook.com
A subspace W of a symplectic vector space (V,Ω) is isotropic when Ω∣W×W​=0. It has at most half the dimension of V; equality makes it a Lagrangian subspace. This use of isotropic concerns an alternating bilinear form, rather than an isotropic quadratic form.

Inertia of a bilinear form ((p,q,r))

Bilinear form OurBigBook.com
The inertia of a real symmetric bilinear form is the triple giving the numbers of positive, negative, and zero squares in a diagonalization. Sylvester's law of inertia makes it independent of the chosen basis.

Signature pair of a real symmetric bilinear form ((n+​,n−​))

Words: 73
Inertia of a bilinear form OurBigBook.com
For a real symmetric bilinear form, let n+​ and n−​ be the dimensions of its positive and negative diagonal subspaces. This pair gives the first two components of the inertia of a bilinear form and is independent of basis by the Sylvester's law of inertia. For a nondegenerate form their sum is the full dimension; otherwise the nullity is an additional invariant. Another convention calls the difference n+​−n−​ the signature of a quadratic form. The pair convention describes the positive and negative harmonic spaces of the real de Rham intersection form in dimension four.

A complex sesquilinear form is linear in one argument and conjugate-linear in the other. Here the first argument is taken to be linear.

Orthogonal complement for a sesquilinear form (W⊥={v:B(v,w)=0 for all w∈W})

Sesquilinear form OurBigBook.com
For a Hermitian form or a Hermitian form over a quadratic finite field, the displayed subspace is the orthogonal complement of W. If the form restricts nondegenerately to a finite-dimensional W, its invertible Gram matrix supplies, for each v, a unique w0​∈W with B(v−w0​,W)=0. Consequently V=W⊕W⊥. When the form on V is nondegenerate, its restriction to W⊥ is too: a radical vector there is orthogonal to both summands and hence is zero.

Hermitian form over a quadratic finite field (B(v,w)=B(w,v)​,aˉ=aq)

Hermitian form OurBigBook.com
Over the finite field K=Fq2​, a sesquilinear form relative to a↦aq is linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its second. It is Hermitian when B(w,v)=B(v,w)​. Its diagonal values belong to Fq​; it is nondegenerate when B(v,w)=0 for every w forces v=0. This definition applies in characteristic two as well.
Hermitian hyperbolic plane over a finite field ((01​10​))

Hermitian form over a quadratic finite field OurBigBook.com
In a two-dimensional nondegenerate Hermitian form over a quadratic finite field, choose an orthonormal basis v,w and a with aaˉ=−1. Then e=v+aw is an isotropic vector. Choose g with B(e,g)=1, and choose c with c+cˉ=B(g,g). The vector f=g−ce satisfies B(e,f)=1 and B(f,f)=0. Thus e,f give the displayed matrix, including in characteristic two. Iterating on nondegenerate orthogonal complement for a sesquilinear form leaves only a unit-norm line in odd dimension.
Orthonormalization of a finite-field Hermitian form
Words: 44
Hermitian form over a quadratic finite field OurBigBook.com
A nondegenerate Hermitian form over a quadratic finite field has an orthonormal basis. If all diagonal values vanished, evaluating B(v+aw,v+aw) would give Tr(aˉB(v,w))=0 for every a, contradicting quadratic finite-field norm and trace surjectivity and nondegeneracy. Thus some v has nonzero norm; rescaling using the field norm makes it one. Its orthogonal complement for a sesquilinear form is nondegenerate, so induction completes the basis.

Monomial orthonormal basis on the unit torus (⟨zα,zβ⟩=δαβ​)

Words: 59
Hermitian form OurBigBook.com
Integrate a polynomial times the conjugate of another over the product of unit circles, with normalized product angular measure. Fourier orthogonality makes the monomials z1α1​​⋯zdαd​​ an orthonormal basis of the polynomial vector space. The Hermitian form is positive definite because the squared norm is the sum of squared absolute values of the finitely many coefficients. No completion or infinite series is needed to obtain this algebraic basis.

Radical of a Hermitian form (radh={v:h(v,w)=0 for all w})

Words: 65
Hermitian form OurBigBook.com
The radical of a Hermitian form is the vector subspace orthogonal to the entire space. The form descends to the quotient vector space by its radical: adding a radical vector to either argument does not change the value. For a positive semidefinite Hermitian form, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality identifies this radical with its zero-norm vectors, so the quotient form is positive definite. This conclusion does not hold for a general indefinite Hermitian form: a zero-norm vector need not belong to its radical.

Positive semidefinite Hermitian form (h(v,v)≥0)

Words: 79
Hermitian form OurBigBook.com
A Hermitian form is positive semidefinite when h(v,v)≥0 for every vector. It need not define an inner product, because a nonzero vector may have zero squared norm. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality still holds: applying nonnegativity to v+zw and minimizing the quadratic expression in z gives ∣h(v,w)∣2≤h(v,v)h(w,w) when h(w,w)>0; when h(w,w)=0, varying z forces h(v,w)=0. Thus its zero-norm vectors are exactly the radical of a Hermitian form. Quotienting this radical of a Hermitian form gives a positive inner product; taking its Hilbert space completion then gives a Hilbert space. This is the final positivity step in the Gupta-Bleuler null-state quotient.

Rotational symmetry group of a regular icosahedron

Words: 89
Rotational symmetry OurBigBook.com
The orientation-preserving rotational symmetry group of a regular icosahedron has order sixty. Its conjugacy classes have sizes 1,15,20,12,12: identity; half-turns about opposite-edge axes; rotations through ±2π/3 about opposite-face axes; and rotations through ±2π/5 and ±4π/5 about opposite-vertex axes, respectively. Conjugation carries an axis to its rotated axis and preserves the rotation angle. The transitive group action on edges, faces and vertices gives the indicated classes, with reversal of the axis identifying the two signs. A normal subgroup must contain whole conjugacy classes; none of the proper nonidentity sums of these class sizes is a divisor of sixty. Thus this group is a simple group.

Rotational symmetry group of a regular dodecahedron (Rot(D)≅A5​)

Words: 179
Rotational symmetry OurBigBook.com
The rotations in three dimensions preserving a dodecahedron form a group of order 60. There are 24 nonidentity rotations about the six axes through opposite face centres, 20 about the ten axes through opposite vertices, and 15 half-turns about the fifteen axes through opposite edge midpoints. Its nonidentity conjugacy classes have sizes 12,12,20,15: the centralizer of a rotation of order five or three consists of rotations about its oriented axis and has order five or three, respectively, while all edge half-turns are conjugate. A normal subgroup is a union of whole conjugacy classes containing the identity. No proper nontrivial sum of these class sizes plus one divides 60, proving that it is a simple group. The centralizers of the fifteen involutions are five distinct Klein four-groups, each containing three involutions. Conjugation permutes these five subgroups nontrivially. The kernel is a normal subgroup, so simplicity makes this nontrivial action injective. Its sign map to a group of order two must be trivial, since simplicity would otherwise force an impossible injection of sixty elements into two. Thus its image lies in the alternating group A5​, and equality of orders makes the image all of A5​.

For compatible matrices P,Q,R, the inequality is rank(PQ)+rank(QR)≤rank(Q)+rank(PQR). One proof uses the block matrix M=(PQQ​0QR​). Subtract P times its lower block row from its upper block row and then subtract its first block column times R from its second. The result is (0Q​−PQR0​), with rank rank(Q)+rank(PQR). On the other hand, choose independent columns of PQ from the first block column and independent columns of QR from the second. The corresponding columns of M are independent: project a relation onto the upper block first, and then onto the lower block. Thus rank(M)≥rank(PQ)+rank(QR).

Inner product space ((V,⟨⋅,⋅⟩))

Words: 63
Inner product OurBigBook.com
An inner product space is a real or complex vector space equipped with a positive-definite inner product. Over the real numbers the form is symmetric and bilinear; over the complex numbers it is conjugate symmetric and sesquilinear. It defines the norm ∥v∥=⟨v,v⟩​. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality proves the triangle inequality for this norm. A complete inner product space is a Hilbert space; every finite-dimensional inner product space is complete.

Gram matrix OurBigBook.com
For n≥2, the Gram matrix of n unit vectors with common distinct-pair inner product t is G=(1−t)I+t11T. Its eigenvalues are 1+(n−1)t on the all-ones direction and 1−t on its orthogonal complement. It is a positive-definite symmetric matrix exactly when −1/(n−1)<t<1, permitting a linearly independent realization in Rn. An explicit construction takes the columns of
B=1−t​(I−uuT)+1+(n−1)t​uuT,u=1/n​.
(37)

Positive-diagonal QR decomposition preserves a complex structure
Words: 94
QR decomposition OurBigBook.com
Let K be block diagonal with 2×2 blocks J=(0−1​10​). If a real invertible matrix A commutes with K, its QR decomposition A=BC, with B orthogonal and C upper triangular with positive diagonal, has both BK=KB and CK=KC. Indeed CKC−1=B−1KB, so E=K−1CKC−1 is orthogonal and upper triangular in 2×2 blocks. Orthogonality forces its off-diagonal blocks to vanish. Its diagonal blocks are J−1Ci​JCi−1​. For Ci​=(a0​bd​) with a,d>0, this block is (d/a−b/a​−b/a(a2+b2)/(ad)​). Orthogonality of its columns forces b=0,d=a, and hence each block is the identity. Thus E=I, proving the claim.
Thin QR factorization from Cholesky decomposition (A=QR,QTQ=I,RTR=ATA)
Words: 74
QR decomposition OurBigBook.com
If a real m-by-n matrix A has full column rank, with m≥n, then ATA is positive-definite. Its upper-triangular Cholesky decomposition ATA=RTR, with positive diagonal, is unique. Defining Q=AR−1 gives QTQ=I and A=QR. Any other such factorization yields another Cholesky factor of ATA, so its R and then its Q must agree. This proves existence and uniqueness; it does not assert that forming ATA is the most numerically stable algorithm.

Local isotropy of the five seven thirteen form (5x2+7y2+13z2)
Words: 98
Isotropy of nondegenerate ternary quadratic forms over finite fields OurBigBook.com
This ternary quadratic form has a nonzero zero over Qp​ exactly when p=7. Away from 2,5,7,13, the finite-field square-set intersection proof supplies a nonsingular residue zero, and Hensel lemma lifts it. At 5 use (0,1,1) modulo 5; at 13 use (3,1,0). At 2 hold x=2,z=1 and apply the strong form of Hensel lemma to 7Y2+33 at Y=1: the function and derivative have valuations 3 and 1. At 7, the equation modulo 7 forces x=z=0 because 5 is not a square; reduction after dividing by 7 then forces y=0. Any normalized integral nonzero solution would therefore have all coordinates divisible by 7, a contradiction.

Criterion for membership in a diagonal basis

Words: 70
Sylvester's law of inertia OurBigBook.com
A vector v can be included in a diagonal basis for a real quadratic form precisely when v=0 and either its quadratic value is nonzero or it lies in the radical of a bilinear form. Conversely, an isotropic vector in a diagonal basis is orthogonal to every basis vector, and must lie in the radical.

For a nondegenerate real quadratic form of inertia (p,q), projection of a totally isotropic subspace onto either its positive or negative coordinate subspace is injective: a vector with one projection zero would have strictly one-signed quadratic value unless it vanished. Totally isotropic subspace OurBigBook.com

Linear algebra OurBigBook.com

Coefficient-dominated entrywise positivity

Words: 89
Schur product theorem OurBigBook.com
Let real power series f(t)=∑k≥0​fk​tk and g(t)=∑k≥0​gk​tk converge on [−1,1], with fk​≥∣gk​∣ for every index including zero. If X⪰0 has entries there, applying f within two diagonal blocks and g across them preserves positive semidefiniteness. Indeed the coefficient matrix Hk​ is a bipartite block-constant positive semidefinite matrix. Each Hk​∘X∘k is positive semidefinite by the Schur product theorem, and their sum converges to the transformed matrix. Closedness of the positive semidefinite cone completes the proof. Convergence at one gives ∑fk​<∞, so coefficient domination ensures absolute convergence of both series throughout the interval. Without the zero-index condition, f=−1, g=0 and X=0 give a counterexample.

Cartan–Dieudonné theorem

Words: 72
Orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
Every orthogonal transformation of a finite-dimensional nondegenerate quadratic space over a field of characteristic different from two is a product of at most its dimension many hyperplane reflections. In the real positive-definite case, a reflection normal to gv−v sends gv to v whenever gv=v. Composing with that reflection fixes v and leaves an orthogonal transformation of v⊥, so induction proves the bound. Each reflection has determinant minus one, hence orientation-preserving transformations use an even number of reflections.

Determinant-twist projection in odd dimension (π(A)=(detA)A)

Words: 65
Orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
For real orthogonal matrices in odd dimension d, multiplying by their determinant defines a group homomorphism from O(d) onto SO(d). Scalar factors commute, so π(AB)=π(A)π(B), while detπ(A)=(detA)d+1=1. The map fixes SO(d) and has kernel {I,−I}. Since −I is central and has determinant −1 in odd dimension, O(d)≅SO(d)×C2​. In even dimension the same expression does not map every orthogonal matrix into the special orthogonal group.

Words: 60
Orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
In odd dimension, the map A↦(detA)A is a surjective group homomorphism from the orthogonal group to the special orthogonal group, with kernel of a group homomorphism {I,−I}. Scalar matrices commute, and det[(detA)A]=(detA)2m+2=1. Together with the determinant sign, it identifies O(2m+1) with the direct product of groups SO(2m+1)×C2​. In even dimension, scalar multiplication by detA does not repair the determinant, so this construction does not give the same splitting.

A real orthogonal matrix T of size three with detT=−1 has an eigenvector n of eigenvalue −1. Words: 70
Special orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
All the special orthogonal groups are connected, and their second homotopy groups vanish. The rotation circle gives SO(2)≅S1. Conjugation by unit quaternions gives the twofold universal cover S3→SO(3), so π1​SO(3)=Z/2 and π3​SO(3)=Z. The special orthogonal sphere fibration SO(n−1)→SO(n)→Sn−1 propagates the first two homotopy groups for n≥4. In dimension four its exact sequence has a zero map from the torsion group π4​S3=Z/2 to π3​SO(3)=Z, giving π3​SO(4)=Z2. For SO(1) all positive groups vanish, and π3​SO(2)=0.

Words: 108 Articles: 1
Special orthogonal group OurBigBook.com
The last-column map p(A)=Aes+1​ has fiber SO(s), included as diag(B,1). Local completion of a unit vector by the Gram-Schmidt process gives local fiber bundle charts. Consequently it has the homotopy lifting property and the long exact sequence of homotopy groups of a fibration.
Surjectivity of special orthogonal stabilization below the sphere dimension (πr​(SO(s))↠πr​(SO(s+1))(r<s))
Words: 78
Special orthogonal sphere fibration OurBigBook.com
Project a based map α:Sr→SO(s+1) to Ss. Since r<s, the resulting homotopy class vanishes. Lift a based null-homotopy by the special orthogonal sphere fibration. Its endpoint lies in the fiber SO(s). If the lift moves its base point, right-multiply at time t by the inverse of its base-point value, which lies in the fiber. This keeps the projected homotopy unchanged and makes the lift based. Thus α is based-homotopic to a map into SO(s), proving the asserted surjectivity.

The SO(4) group consists of real orthogonal four-by-four matrices of determinant one. It preserves orientation and the Euclidean metric. Its Spin(4) double cover identifies it with the quotient of two copies of SU(2) by their simultaneous central sign.

Their dimensions are (2jL​+1)(2jR​+1). Under the diagonal spatial rotation subgroup, the Clebsch-Gordan decomposition for SU2 gives spins from ∣jL​−jR​∣ through jL​+jR​ in steps of one.
